Learn Japanese from Scratch: A Flexible Roadmap

Kanjidon Team · Jan 31, 2026

A useful beginner roadmap does not promise fluency by a date or require one perfect resource. It connects the skills needed for your goal, tests them in real tasks and changes when the evidence changes. Use the stages below as movable layers, not a fixed calendar.

First, Name the Situation You Want to Handle

  • Travel: understand signs, basic questions and routine transactions.
  • Conversation: follow and produce exchanges on familiar topics.
  • Reading: move from supported texts toward the genres you care about.
  • Work or study: build the vocabulary, register and feedback required by that setting.
  • JLPT: prepare for the official language knowledge, reading and listening formats.

The goal decides what deserves more time. A reading-focused learner can prioritize recognition; someone who must complete forms or write by hand needs more production practice. No single sequence fits all five situations equally.

Layer One: Kana, Sound and Survival Phrases

  • Learn hiragana and katakana through short words and phrases.
  • Connect spelling to clear audio, including long vowels and small kana.
  • Practise greetings, self-introduction and questions that fit your goal.
  • Reduce romaji as kana decoding becomes usable.

Layer Two: Grammar and Vocabulary in Context

Use short sentences to learn how Japanese marks topic, participants, time, negation and politeness. Store vocabulary with pronunciation and one useful context. Grammar explanations help, but comprehension and production tasks reveal whether you can use the pattern.

Layer Three: Kanji Through Words

Introduce kanji inside vocabulary you are already learning. Ask for one target at a time: recognize the word, retrieve its reading or understand it in a sentence. Components and handwriting can support memory, but avoid memorizing every possible reading before the words that use it.

Layer Four: Listening and Reading from the Start

  • Choose short material with audio, transcript, glossary or other support you can gradually remove.
  • Attempt the main idea before looking up details.
  • Replay or reread after identifying the specific obstacle.
  • Move across topics so familiarity with one script does not masquerade as general comprehension.
  • Keep some input for enjoyment, not only analysis.

Layer Five: Output and Feedback

Speaking and writing become useful when the task has a purpose and feedback. Record a short response, write a message or practise an exchange, then ask for correction on a defined point. The JLPT does not directly assess these skills, so include them explicitly if they belong to your goal.

Run an Adaptive Study Cycle

StepQuestion
ChooseWhat small real-world ability am I building next?
LearnWhich words, kanji and grammar does that ability require?
RetrieveCan I produce the target before seeing the answer?
ApplyCan I understand or use it in fresh material?
AdjustWhich repeated error should change the next cycle?

Start with Reliable, Current Resources

The Japan Foundation publishes official learning materials that can provide a structured starting point. If the JLPT is part of your goal, use its official level descriptions and samples to understand what the exam actually measures. Product features, prices and availability can change, so verify them on the current official page before building your plan around them.

Official Learning Sources

  • Japan Foundation directory of Japanese learning materials
  • Japan Foundation Irodori learning materials
  • Official JLPT level descriptions
  • Official JLPT sample questions and practice workbooks
